newsitem.title: UK: Adams offers "sympathy" to N.Irish bomb victims.
newsitem.headline: Adams offers "sympathy" to N.Irish bomb victims.

text.p: Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political wing, on Tuesday offered his sympathy to the victims of a double car bomb attack on Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters and said his party remained committed to peace.

"Can I begin by expressing my sympathy to the families of those who were injured in yesterday's explosions at the British Army headquarters at Lisburn and my sense of shock," Sinn Fein leader Adams told reporters in Belfast.

Adams said he was committed to restoring peace in the Irish Republican Army's 27-year war against British rule of Northern Ireland. A 17-month IRA ceasefire was shattered in February by a bomb in London and Monday's bomb in Northern Ireland further damaged peace hopes.
"My commitment is to help to rebuild peace," he said.

"Even yesterday I was working at that and I haven't stopped working at that since last February and my commitment to work at that today after the explosions is the same and, if anything, more deeply focused than it was yesterday."

Adams said he did not know who carried out the Lisburn barracks blast. A caller to Irish broadcasting network RTE claimed reponsibility for the attack on behalf of a shadowy Republican splinter group, the Continuity Army Council.
But analysts said they were sceptical of this claim and the British government, Northern Irish police and security forces said the IRA was the main suspect.

Adams said he did not believe the attack had been designed to provoke Protestant loyalist guerrillas, who want Northern Ireland to stay British, into abandoning their two-year ceasefire and returning to violence.

"I think when we reflect about what provoking Loyalists means, it means the wholesale slaughter of Catholics, it means the killing of members of our party, of our family members or of our activists and I dont think anyone would try to provoke that kind of action," he said.
He called for Sinn Fein's inclusion in multi-party peace talks taking place in Belfast. The party is currently barred because the IRA refuses to renounce violence.
"I am prepared to go today and enter into talks with the British government, with the various other parties to try and find a way out of this vacuum," he said. "That includes the loyalists."
